notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Deuteronomy 31, drawn from the sources I could access within the search and fetch limits:

---

## Deuteronomy 31 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — "When Moses had finished speaking these words to all Israel…"

- **The meaning of "went and spoke":** Ellicott notes the Hebrew expression is unusual; it may mean "went on to speak." The LXX reads "Moses made an end of speaking," possibly reflecting a slightly different Hebrew text. The Targum of Jonathan says he "went to the tabernacle of the house of doctrine" and spoke. Aben Ezra suggests he went to each tribe separately to inform them he was about to die. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** says the phrase means Moses "disposed or set himself" to speak — a deliberate, arranged action, not a casual one. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Gill** suggests Moses had dismissed the people after the covenant renewal ceremony (ch. 29–30) and now summoned them again, likely at the tabernacle. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-31.html)

### v. 2 — "I am now a hundred and twenty years old; I am no longer able to come and go, and the LORD has said to me, 'You shall not cross the Jordan.'"

- **Guzik (Enduring Word)** argues that Moses was not physically incapacitated — Deuteronomy 34:7 says his eye was undimmed and his vigor unabated. Rather, he was limited by God's decree. His inability to "come and go" refers to his leadership role being ended by God, not physical frailty. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-31/)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** disagrees: Moses may well have felt himself failing internally even though observers saw no decline. They cite the common experience that a person senses their own weakening before others notice it. They reject the reading that makes God's prohibition the *cause* of Moses saying he could no longer lead; rather, these are two independent reasons. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Gill** concurs with Guzik: Moses' inability was not bodily but because "it was the will of God that he should live no longer to exercise such an office." Gill specifically notes that Moses' law could not bring anyone into the heavenly Canaan — only Jesus (Joshua) and His righteousness can. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Guzik** adds that God's correction of Moses was severe: not merely losing leadership but being barred from entering Canaan at all. At Meribah, Moses misrepresented God by striking the rock twice instead of speaking to it, defacing the picture of Christ — who needs to be struck only once (1 Cor 10:4; Heb 10:10–12). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-31/)

### v. 3 — "The LORD your God Himself will cross over ahead of you. He will destroy these nations before you… Joshua will cross ahead of you, as the LORD has said."

- **Ellicott** observes a remarkable textual detail: in Hebrew, "Jehovah, He is going over; Joshua, he is going over" — the two are spoken of in exactly parallel language, with no conjunction between them (the English "and" is supplied). He sees this as a "prophetical truth" identifying Yahweh and Joshua in a typological way, much like "the God who fed me… the Angel that redeemed me" in Genesis 48:15–16. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Guzik** emphasizes that Moses was not irreplaceable: "God being with them, Israel was in good hands, with or without Moses." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-31/)
- **Precept Austin** (from search excerpt) notes the truth that the LORD goes before is repeated three times (vv. 3, 6, 8), and that the verb for "dispossess" (*yarash*) is the same as "possess" — "dispossess them so you can possess their land." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-31-commentary)

### v. 4 — "And the LORD will do to them as He did to Sihon and Og, the kings of the Amorites…"

- **Ellicott** says the value of these two conquests before crossing the Jordan "was inestimable, as an encouragement to them to persevere." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Gill** adds that this reference was to "encourage their faith, assuring them that what had been done to them would be done to the Canaanitish kings." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-31.html)

### v. 5 — "The LORD will deliver them over to you, and you must do to them exactly as I have commanded you."

- **Gill** says "as I have commanded" refers to the commands to utterly destroy them, make no covenant, enter no marriages, demolish altars, cut down groves, and break images (Deut 7:1–5). The Targum of Jonathan interprets "the Word of the Lord shall deliver them up." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Ellicott** notes the Hebrew word for "commandments" here is singular — *mitzvah* — meaning "the principle of action." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-31.html)

### v. 6 — "Be strong and courageous; do not be afraid or terrified of them, for it is the LORD your God who goes with you; He will never leave you nor forsake you."

- **Gill** notes the Septuagint renders this "play the men, and be strong." He connects it to 1 Corinthians 16:13 and Hebrews 13:5 — the promise is made to literal Israel but "belongs to the spiritual Israel of God, and is made good to every true believer in the Lord." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Guzik** notes Trapp's observation: "Five times in holy Scriptures is this precious promise repeated; and in Hebrews 13:5, made common to all believers." This is the first of seven times that "be strong and courageous" appears directed to or involving Joshua (vv. 6, 7, 23; Josh 1:6, 7, 9, 18). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-31/)
- **The Reformed perspective (Ligonier / R.C. Sproul):** The pledge of covenant presence "is a promise given to us today through Christ (Heb. 13:5). Still, we should see that it is a promise to be with us and not a promise to keep our lives free from harm, calamity, or suffering." God does not promise we will always *feel* His presence — feelings do not determine the truth of His Word. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/be-strong-and-courageous)
- **Desiring God (John Piper, Baptist):** Uses Deuteronomy 31:8 as a key promise for battling the unbelief of anxiety: "You deal with anxieties by battling unbelief. And you battle unbelief by meditating on God's word and asking for the help of his Spirit." He cites this verse as a "windshield wiper" promise that clears away the mud of unbelief. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/battling-the-unbelief-of-anxiety)
- **Ellicott** notes the exhortation here is addressed to the *people* in the plural; the same words are addressed to Joshua individually in the next verse. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-31.html)

### v. 7 — "Then Moses called for Joshua and said to him in the presence of all Israel, 'Be strong and courageous…'"

- **Gill** says this was done "in the sight of all Israel… to make him the more respectable to them." Joshua was already a man of proven courage (Exodus 17:9, the battle with Amalek), yet the exhortation was not needless given the work ahead. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Guzik** notes that Moses "knew that Joshua might be wavering, so he encouraged him, and pushed him forward to fulfill the great calling God gave to him. God uses encouraging people to help His people fulfill their destiny." He also notes David later used these same words to urge Solomon to build the temple (1 Chron 22:13; 28:20). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-31/)
- **Garner-Howes (Baptist):** This occasion was likely a later, more public ceremony than the earlier appointment in Numbers 27:18–23. Moses publicly encouraged Joshua to be courageous and fearless. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/deuteronomy-31.html)

### v. 8 — "The LORD Himself goes before you; He will be with you. He will never leave you nor forsake you. Do not be afraid or discouraged."

- **Gill** notes the Targum renders "the LORD" as "the Word of the Lord, his Shechinah" — the same who brought Israel out of Egypt and went before them in the wilderness. "He will not fail thee" means "not fail to give him counsel and direction, to afford him strength… nor forsake him till he had finished the work." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Ellicott** observes that "He will not fail thee, neither forsake thee" is the exact promise repeated by Jehovah Himself in Joshua 1:5. "Will not let thee go" is the precise meaning of "fail" here — compare Deuteronomy 9:14, "let me alone." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Precept Austin** (from search excerpt) highlights the threefold repetition of the LORD going before (vv. 3, 6, 8), which would encourage Joshua that he was not solely responsible for success — the LORD "had his back." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-31-commentary)

### vv. 9–13 — The Writing and Reading of the Law

**v. 9 — "So Moses wrote down this law and gave it to the priests, the sons of Levi, who carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD, and to all the elders of Israel."**

- **Ellicott** distinguishes this from the later delivery of the "book" to the Levites in vv. 25–26. Here it is a "charge and a trust conveyed to the priests, making them responsible for the 'reading of the law,' and for the instruction of the people." The priests "bore" the ark in the sense of being responsible for it, not always physically carrying it. This also illustrates the distinction between priests and Levites in Deuteronomy. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Gill** says "this law" means the book of Deuteronomy or the whole Pentateuch. He notes the Jewish tradition that Moses wrote thirteen copies — twelve for the twelve tribes, and one to be placed in the ark. The law was given to both spiritual leaders (priests) and civil leaders (elders). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Guzik** says commentators debate whether "this law" means all five books of Moses, only Deuteronomy, or just the summary in chapter 31. Kalland is cited: "Most of the material in chapter 31 is given elsewhere in Deuteronomy. This material appears to be in the nature of a summary." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-31/)

**v. 10 — "At the end of every seven years, at the appointed time in the year of remission of debt, during the Feast of Tabernacles…"**

- **Gill** discusses a debate about timing: the Mishnah (Sotah 7:8) places it at the *close* of the seventh year, on the eighth year coming in. But Aben Ezra interprets it as the *beginning* of the seventh year, which Gill favors because the Feast of Tabernacles is in the month Tishri, which was the original beginning of the year for release purposes. It was a fitting time: all harvest was gathered in, there was no tillage (it being a sabbatical year), and debtors were released and free from care. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-31.html)

**v. 11 — "…you are to read this law in the hearing of all Israel."**

- **Gill** notes the question of *who* reads: Josephus ascribes it to the high priest; Jewish writers generally assign it to the king or supreme governor. The Mishnah describes the king reading select portions from Deuteronomy (from 1:1 through sections on the Shema, blessings and curses, and the section on the king). Joshua read the law (Josh 8:35), as did Josiah (2 Kings 23:2) and Ezra (Neh 8:3). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Ellicott** confirms from the Talmud (tractate Sotah, p. 41) that the reading began with Deuteronomy 1:1, and that King Agrippa wept when he reached Deuteronomy 17:15 ("you may not set a stranger over you"), but the people reassured him, "Fear not, Agrippa, thou art our brother." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-31.html)

**v. 12 — "Assemble the people — men, women, children, and the foreigners within your gates…"**

- **Gill** notes this was distinctive: at the three annual festivals, only males were obligated to appear; women could come voluntarily. But for this seventh-year reading, *all* — every age and sex — were summoned, including the resident alien ("the stranger that is within thy gates"), whether proselyte of righteousness or merely a "proselyte of the gate" who had renounced idolatry. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** emphasizes that the object was not merely to inform but to publicly declare and impress the covenantal conditions of their national life. At the Feast of Tabernacles — celebrating deliverance from wilderness wandering and settlement in the land — they were reminded of the law on which their continued blessing depended. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-31.html)

**v. 13 — "Then their children who do not know the law will listen and learn to fear the LORD your God…"**

- **Ellicott** notes: "It is obvious from this that the existence of many copies of the law was not contemplated by the writer." The public reading was essential because individual families did not possess their own copies. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Gill** says the purpose was that children "may hear the law of God, learn the meaning of it, and so be brought up in the fear, nurture, and admonition of the Lord." This was a means to perpetuate fear and worship of God in their posterity and thereby secure their long continuance in the land. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Guzik** observes that the public reading was "especially important for the children" — through the proclaimed word, they could "come to a personal relationship with the LORD." He also notes the known public readings (Josh 8:30–35; 2 Chron 17:7–9 under Jehoshaphat, about 500 years later; 2 Chron 34:30 under Josiah, 250 more years later) were likely unusual rather than regular, and "if… the word of the LORD was so neglected by the Levites… no wonder Israel was so often in trouble." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-31/)

### v. 14 — "Then the LORD said to Moses, 'Behold, the time of your death is near. Call Joshua and present yourselves at the Tent of Meeting, so that I may commission him.'"

- **Ellicott** compares this to the transfer of priesthood from Aaron to Eleazar on Mount Hor (Num 20:25–28) and Elijah and Elisha crossing Jordan together (2 Kings 2). This was the last recorded occasion of Jehovah meeting Moses face to face in the tabernacle; their next meeting was on Mount Nebo, and the next "within the veil." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Guzik** notes Joshua's qualification for leadership: "Joshua had a real relationship with God, and he was at home in the presence of the LORD," having often been at the tabernacle with Moses (Ex 33:11). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-31/)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** explains the Hebrew: "that I may give him a charge" — the verb means to constitute, appoint, and confirm him in office. What Moses had done publicly (vv. 1–8) is now ratified directly by Jehovah. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-31.html)

### v. 15 — "Then the LORD appeared at the tent in a pillar of cloud, and the cloud stood over the entrance to the tent."

- **The Pulpit Commentary** cross-references Exodus 33:9; 40:38; Leviticus 16:2; Numbers 12:5 for similar theophanies. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Gill** notes the Targum of Jonathan adds that "Moses and Joshua stood without" — outside the tabernacle — while the pillar of cloud stood over the door. The cloud had a visible glory showing God's presence. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Guzik** says the visible presence marked the solemn importance of this retirement ceremony for Moses and inauguration for Joshua. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-31/)

### v. 16 — "You will soon rest with your fathers, and these people will rise up and prostitute themselves with the foreign gods of the land…"

- **Gill** explains "sleep with thy fathers" as a phrase expressive of death, used of both good and bad, which "serves to render death easy and familiar, and less formidable; and to assure and lead into an expectation of an awaking out of it, or a resurrection from it." He notes the people would "rise up" in their posterity — the revolt to idolatry (Judges 2:17–19) came after Joshua's death. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** adds that "go a whoring" (Ex 34:15; Judg 2:17) refers to idolatry as spiritual adultery, violating the covenant which had the nature of a matrimonial contract (Jer 31:32). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Ellicott** draws a striking theological parallel: God knew the risk of choosing Israel and "provided for it beforehand" — just as at creation He provided redemption through Christ before the fall in Genesis 3. "God brought Israel into Canaan in full foreknowledge of what the people would become when there." He contrasts Judges 2:1 ("I will never break my covenant with you") with 2 Timothy 2:13: "If we believe not, yet He abideth faithful." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-31.html)

### vv. 17–18 — God's anger, hiding His face, and Israel's troubles

- **Gill** explains "I will forsake them" means withdrawing favours and protection; "hide My face" means taking no notice of them in providence for good, nor hearing their cries to deliver them. The confession "Is it not because our God is not among us?" shows they would recognize the *fact* of God's absence but gives "no intimation of their being sensible of their sins as the cause." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Guzik** and **Kalland** explain "hiding His face" as the opposite of the Aaronic blessing of Numbers 6:25–26 — the reversal of making His face shine upon them. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-31/)
- **Ellicott** cites Rashi: "I will surely hide my face" means "as though I did not see them in their distress." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Garner-Howes (Baptist):** Clarifies that verse 17 "does not teach that God would forsake Israel. It means that He would withdraw His favor and help from them, and allow their enemies to invade." Trouble brought temporary repentance and return to God, but "it was not a permanent restoration." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/deuteronomy-31.html)

### v. 19 — "Now therefore, write down for yourselves this song and teach it to the Israelites; have them recite it, so that it may be a witness for Me against them."

- **Ellicott** explains the method: "It was not possible to multiply copies of the law among them to any great extent; but the rhythmical form of the song would make it easy to be retained in their memories." He suggests Samuel later employed the same method — psalms and spiritual songs — through the companies of prophets (1 Sam 10:5–6; 19:20–24), using historical psalms like 78, 105, and 106 as "a very efficacious means of spreading the knowledge of God." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Guzik** says "put it in their mouths" implies sufficient repetition to fix it in memory. He quotes Morgan: "Songs often remain after commandments are forgotten." Clarke adds: "Things which were of great importance and of common concern were, among the ancients, put into verse, as this was found the best method of keeping them in remembrance." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-31/)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** says both Moses and Joshua were to write the song — Moses as author, Joshua as his amanuensis — because both were to do their part to keep the people from apostasy. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-31.html)

### vv. 20–21 — Prosperity leading to apostasy, the song as a lasting witness

- **Gill** explains the sequence: after eating their fill and growing fat (prosperity), Israel would turn to other gods. The song "will testify against them as a witness; for it will not be forgotten in the mouths of their descendants." The song would show they had been "sufficiently warned, and might have lived to God, and so escaped those disasters." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Ellicott** notes that the Hebrew word for "imagination" (v. 21) is *yêtzer*, the same word used in Genesis 6:5 and 8:21 — the word commonly used in rabbinical literature for the evil or good inclination in a person. He observes the paradox: God knew their evil *yêtzer*, yet He also had Balaam say, "He hath not beheld iniquity in Jacob" (Num 23:21). He cross-references Psalm 103:14: "He knoweth our frame (*yêtzer*); He remembereth that we are dust." Rashi comments on v. 21: "This is a promise to Israel that the law shall not be utterly forgotten by their seed." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-31.html)

### v. 22 — "So that very day Moses wrote down this song and taught it to the Israelites."

- **Guzik** notes the irony: "This was a strange national song, because the purpose of this anthem was to testify against Israel as a witness." The song reminded them of the covenant pledges and judgments they had voluntarily invoked upon themselves. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-31/)

### v. 23 — "Then the LORD commissioned Joshua son of Nun and said, 'Be strong and courageous…'"

- **Ellicott** highlights: "This is the first record of God's direct communion with Joshua." Joshua had been with Moses on the mount and in the tabernacle (Ex 24:13; 33:11), but no divine communication to Joshua apart from Moses is recorded before this moment. It ratifies his appointment. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Guzik** provides an extended profile of Joshua's qualifications: led the army against Amalek, assistant to Moses, faithful at the tabernacle after the golden calf, zealous for Moses' authority, one of two faith-filled spies, and "a man in whom is the Spirit" (Num 27:18). The name Yehoshua (Joshua) is the same as Iesous (Jesus) in Greek — "The Conqueror of Canaan and the Redeemer of the world bear the same name" (Maclaren). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-31/)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** clarifies that the subject of "he gave Joshua… a charge" in v. 23 is *God*, not Moses, as shown by "the land which *I* swore unto them; and *I* will be with thee" (cf. Ex 3:12). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-31.html)

### vv. 24–26 — Completion of the Book of the Law; placement beside the ark

- **Ellicott** says "when Moses had made an end of writing" refers to the completion of *all* the books of Moses as delivered to Israel — not merely Deuteronomy (as in v. 9), but the whole Pentateuch, including the song. The song was probably the final section. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Gill** notes the Book was placed "in the side of the ark" — meaning *beside* it. He cites the Talmud (Baba Bathra) where rabbis debated: some said there was a shelf or slab projecting from the ark where the book rested; others said it was placed inside the ark alongside the tablets of the covenant. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Ellicott** adds that Rashi recorded the same rabbinic dispute. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Guzik** clarifies: the Ten Commandments were *inside* the ark (Heb 9:4); the whole Book of the Law was placed *beside* the ark. Merrill is quoted: "The holy of holies thus became a kind of sacred archives housing the documents that attested to the Lord's relationship to his people." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-31/)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** discusses whether this section was written by Moses or added later as an appendix, concluding it is "quite possible" Moses recorded this himself before laying down the pen. What follows from v. 30 onward was "probably added to the writing of Moses by someone after his death," though the song (ch. 32) and blessing (ch. 33) are certainly Mosaic compositions. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-31.html)

### v. 27 — "For I know how rebellious and stiff-necked you are…"

- **Guzik** observes that Moses knew Israel would rebel "both from the promise of God (Deuteronomy 31:16-17), and from common sense (If today, while I am yet alive with you, you have been rebellious against the LORD, then how much more after my death?)." The law would stand as a witness against them. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-31/)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** notes the Hebrew word for "rebellion" here is *meri* — "rebelliousness, i.e., tendency to rebel," the same root used in Numbers 17:25 (the people are "sons of rebelliousness"). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-31.html)

### vv. 28–29 — Calling heaven and earth as witnesses; prediction of corruption

- **Ellicott** notes that Joshua similarly gave a special charge to the elders at the close of his life (Joshua 23). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Guzik** says Moses spoke either "by divinely given prophetic insight or through intuition based on experience." Israel stayed generally faithful through Joshua's leadership but turned aside in the days of the Judges, "did do evil, and they did provoke the LORD to anger." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-31/)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** notes "in the latter days" (v. 29) is a common prophetic expression, first appearing in Genesis 49:1, also Numbers 24:14 and Deuteronomy 4:30. Some tie it to "the days of the Messiah," but a comparison of uses "will show that it cannot be tied strictly to any one period." "The work of your hands" may refer specifically to idols (cf. Deut 4:28) or to evil deeds in general. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-31.html)
- **Precept Austin** notes Moses calls three witnesses in this chapter: (1) the Song (vv. 19, 21), (2) the Law beside the Ark (v. 26), and (3) heaven and earth (v. 28). Two witnesses would have been sufficient to convict (Deut 19:15). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-31-commentary)
- **Thompson** (cited by Guzik) observes that the song of Deuteronomy 32 resembles "a well-known secular political form, namely, the formulation of a complaint against a rebel vassal by his overlord with the threat of punishment" — a form Moses would have known from Pharaoh's court. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-31/)

### v. 30 — "Then Moses recited aloud to the whole assembly of Israel the words of this song from beginning to end."

- **Ellicott** observes: "The exodus of Israel begins and ends with a song of Moses." The song of Exodus 15 is usually called the "Song of Moses" (Rev 15:3–4), but "there is a remarkable resemblance between Revelation 15:3 and Deuteronomy 32:3–4." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-31.html)

---

## Denominational Distinctives Noted

**Baptist (Gill, Garner-Howes, Piper):**
- Gill sees the law placed beside the ark as a type: Christ alone, not Moses' law, brings believers into the heavenly Canaan — a strongly Christocentric, grace-oriented Baptist reading. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-31.html)
- Garner-Howes insists God's "forsaking" in v. 17 means withdrawing favor, not absolute abandonment, preserving a Baptist emphasis on God's faithfulness despite judgment. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/deuteronomy-31.html)
- Piper (Desiring God) applies v. 8 directly to battling anxiety through faith in God's promises — a practical emphasis on sanctification by faith through Scripture meditation. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/battling-the-unbelief-of-anxiety)

**Reformed (Ligonier/Sproul):**
- Emphasizes that God's promise of presence does not guarantee freedom from harm, calamity, or suffering — a Reformed insistence on God's sovereignty in affliction. Also stresses that feelings do not determine the reality of God's presence; faith rests on the Word. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/be-strong-and-courageous)

**Anglican (Ellicott):**
- Noted the typological identification of Jehovah and Joshua in the Hebrew parallelism of v. 3, a characteristically Anglican sensitivity to literary structure and prophetic typology. Also highlighted the paradox of God's foreknowledge of Israel's sin alongside His covenant faithfulness — a nuanced reading of divine sovereignty and human responsibility. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-31.html)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik/Enduring Word):**
- Guzik emphasizes that Joshua was "a man in whom is the Spirit" as the most important qualification of all — the Holy Spirit would empower and enable him. This is a characteristically Pentecostal emphasis on Spirit-empowerment for leadership. Also stresses God using "encouraging people to help His people fulfill their destiny." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-31/)
